svg.title: TicketMaster: full working board, including earlier drafts
svg.desc: Local rendering of live elements from the supplied TicketMaster Excalidraw snapshot. Text, positions, colors and arrow points come from the source. Earlier board drafts may differ from the latest PostgreSQL-authoritative design.

text.tspan: - Booking Table Entry Moved to Reserved State
- Booking service moves creates the Payment order
- Payemnt Order will be returned to the Cliens
- Booking Entry will be moved to COmpleted State
→ { reservationId: R1, userId: U1, orderId: O1 }
Redis owns temporary holds. PostgreSQL is the final authority for confirmed seat allocations.
Scope: reads, booking and recovery. Event creation / seat initialization are deferred.
Read responses return to the client; return arrows omitted. Event details may be cached independently.
No PostgreSQL seat lookup on the normal read path. A seat map is a snapshot, not a reservation guarantee.
2. Reserve selected seats, then create a payment order
Check every selected seat is not sold
No temporary reservation write to PostgreSQL.
Return the payment order / session to the client. The client pays the provider; only verified provider confirmation advances booking.
Creation retries use a stable payment idempotency key. Holds are temporary; they do not guarantee a ticket.
3. Confirm payment: PostgreSQL commit first, then update Redis
Chosen tradeoff: stale Redis may grant a losing hold. PostgreSQL prevents a second confirmed sale; a collected losing payment is refunded.
Do not undo the DB commit
One DB transaction owns all selected seats.
A replay returns the existing booking;
it does not fail just because holds are gone.
The successful customer keeps the ticket
No second confirmed ticket is issued.
If money was collected: persist refund work
and reconcile with the payment provider.
Release only holds owned by the losing booking.
On a sold-seat conflict, repair Redis from DB.
Never delete another customer's hold blindly.
Log / measure the failure; return ticket success.
sold seats to Redis until the update succeeds.
DB is the authority; stale Redis can grant bad holds.
Optional stronger delivery: a PostgreSQL outbox
written in the same booking transaction.
Unknown PostgreSQL commit outcome -> look up booking_id before refunding or retrying. Database unavailable -> no new ticket confirmation.
Verified callbacks and unfinished payment attempts must be durably recorded / reconciled so a service restart does not lose paid work.
4. Redis model: no expiresAt field required
TTL removes the entire hold; no move between seat arrays.
HGETALL / HMGET + batched MGET for hold keys.
Redis Cluster: same-event keys share the {E1} hash tag
so multi-key scripts execute in one slot.
PostgreSQL uniqueness + transaction prevent two confirmed
Stable booking / payment IDs make retries idempotent.
Redis grants temporary holds, not guaranteed tickets.
Stale Redis can lead to a rejected paid attempt and refund.
No claim of strongly consistent seat-map reads.
Gate new holds during recovery. Restore confirmed sold seats
from PostgreSQL before reopening. Reconcile in-flight payments
and lost holds; do not treat an empty Redis as an empty venue.
Use repeatable reconciliation; outbox is an optional mechanism.
Redis errors do not invalidate already-committed tickets.
Event creation and initialization are outside this review.
No Redis Stream / async PostgreSQL confirmation in this version.
One connected diagram; one Redis and one PostgreSQL. Redis is a preliminary gate; PostgreSQL owns actual holds and confirmed bookings.
Solid arrows: application calls. Dashed arrows: fallback / synchronization. Responses return through the caller; most return arrows are omitted.
Not updated for each seat hold
DB hold success required before payment
Callbacks may be duplicated or delayed
Client success page is not confirmation
Try Redis update after the DB commit.
Failure -> log + repair, not ticket failure.
Unknown DB outcome -> look up booking ID.
Never confirm without a known DB commit.
Fallback seat read when Redis is unavailable
Redis Lua script checks not-sold + no active competing hold,
then creates all selected hold keys atomically, or none.
Same-event keys use {E1} for one Redis Cluster slot.
A Redis success is provisional. PostgreSQL must atomically
acquire the same seats before the client gets hold success.
Use status / expiry conditions; versioning can guard updates.
Mirror the DB expiry as the remaining Redis TTL.
DB conflict -> release only this reservation's Redis holds.
Unknown DB outcome -> look up the reservation before release.
No payment -> Redis TTL expires; PostgreSQL treats its expired
reservation as available when reading / acquiring seats.
Payment starts only after the PostgreSQL hold succeeds.
Verified provider success -> Booking Service -> PostgreSQL.
In one transaction, validate live reservation ownership,
confirm the booking and allocate ALL seats, or none.
PostgreSQL prevents two confirmed owners of the same seat.
Replayed callbacks return an already-committed booking.
After commit: update Redis to BOOKED and remove stale holds.
Redis failure does not invalidate the confirmed ticket.
Log / monitor failures; reconciliation repairs Redis from DB.
A PostgreSQL outbox is an optional reliable delivery mechanism.
Expired / replaced hold or confirmed allocation conflict:
no ticket; durably track a refund if payment was collected.
Stale Redis can cause failed attempts, not a second DB sale.
DB commit unknown -> resolve by booking ID before refunding.
No Redis Stream is required in this PostgreSQL-first design.
Seat-map reads fall back to PostgreSQL.
Skip the Redis gate; run the SAME PostgreSQL hold operation.
Every successful hold still passes through PostgreSQL.
Mixed cached / bypass traffic cannot bypass DB ownership.
Use PostgreSQL while Redis is unavailable or rebuilding.
Repopulate Redis from DB-confirmed seats AND unexpired holds.
Do not initialize a missing cache as all seats available.
Conditional refreshes must not overwrite a newer reservation.
Redis absorbs read traffic and competing hold attempts.
PostgreSQL receives all successful holds + payment work.
Use tighter admission limits during an outage if necessary.
Availability / throughput can degrade; ownership must not.
Event creation and booking-window initialization are deferred.
